summary:
We developed FIRESYNC, a web platform that helps communities and fire managers understand where and when fire activity has been detected. To address the Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots challenge, we organized NASA FIRMS detections from both sensors on a shared grid. For each sensor, a cell with one or more detections counts once per day. We aggregate those counts by month to compare the records using a common measure in an interactive historical calendar.

Users can explore seasonal patterns, identify periods of unusually high activity, review recent hotspots, save areas of interest, and find official reporting channels. An interactive lab lets students compare satellite observations and support their conclusions with evidence.

By making satellite records easier to interpret, FIRESYNC helps fire managers across regions decide where and when to focus monitoring and gives communities clearer information when reporting a potential fire.
details:
What FIRESYNC does

FIRESYNC is a web platform that helps communities, fire managers, and students understand where and when satellites have detected fire activity. Users can select a region, compare the same month across years, replay detections day by day, and download the results. They can also review recent hotspots, save areas of interest, and find official reporting channels. An AI assistant helps users navigate the platform and interpret the information they see.

How we addressed the challenge

We downloaded MODIS and VIIRS hotspot records from NASA FIRMS and placed the detections on a shared grid. For each sensor, a cell with one or more detections counts once per day. For example, if VIIRS records three points in a cell and MODIS records one in the same cell on the same day, each sensor contributes one count. We then aggregated the daily counts by month and used the years when both sensors observed the same region to estimate an adjustment between their records. The resulting historical calendar helps users recognize seasonal patterns and identify periods of unusually high activity.

Tools we used

We used NASA FIRMS as our satellite data source, OpenCode and Codex to assist with coding, and Vercel to host the web prototype.

What makes FIRESYNC creative

In our interactive Laboratory, MODIS and VIIRS appear as characters who bring different reports from the same place and month. Users compare the maps, decide what evidence to check, and explain their conclusions. They can then open the same case in FIRESYNC’s sensor comparison view to see how the platform made the records comparable.

Benefits and intended impact

Fire managers can use the historical calendar to decide where and when to prioritize monitoring. Residents can look up the time and location of a hotspot and use that information to report a possible fire through the appropriate official channel. The Laboratory gives students a way to practice interpreting satellite data and supporting conclusions with evidence. The harmonization method can also be tested in other regions to help preserve the continuity of fire activity records as sensors change.

Factors we considered

MODIS and VIIRS differ in spatial resolution, sensitivity, and observation schedules. We designed FIRESYNC to make the basis of the comparison visible, distinguish missing data from periods with zero recorded detections, and label each hotspot as a satellite detection that requires confirmation. Each detection includes its location, time, and sensor so users can assess and share the information with its context.
